1. PURPOSE AND INTRODUCTION
This topical report documents the performance and results of the 50 th Year
(Period 11) Reactor Building In-Service Inspection. Reactor Building (RB) in-
service inspection (ISI) is performed nominally at 5-year intervals following the
initial RB Structural Integrity Test (SIT) to demonstrate the continued structural
integrity of the RB as required by ASME Section XI (2004 Edition), Subsection
IWL, USNRC Regulation 10 CFR 50.55a, and Technical Specification (TS) 4.4.2.
The initial RB SIT was performed at Crane Clean Energy Center (Crane),
formerly Three Mile Island Nuclear Station Unit 1 (TMI-1), on March 9, 1974.
Crane performed its last surveillance, the 40th Year Surveillance, between
September 2013 and February 2014, as documented in Topical Report 213.
Per the rolling 5-year test frequency required by IWL-2410 and IWL-2420 and
allowable 1 year of grace, the 45th Year Surveillance would have been required
at Crane no later than March 9, 2020. In accordance with NRC-approved relief
request RR-18-01 (ML19226A023), the 45th Year Surveillance was authorized to
be limited to only the visual examinations of RB concrete and tendon end
anchorage hardware required by Examination Category L-A and IWL-2510. The
examination and physical testing requirements of Examination Category L-B
were authorized to be deferred to the 50th Year Surveillance. The 50th Year
Surveillance would have been required no later than March 9, 2025. The 50 th
Year Surveillance scope would include both the visual examinations required
under Examination Category L-A and the examinations and physical testing
required under Examination Category L-B. However, on September 20, 2019,
Crane shut down for decommissioning, and on September 26, 2019 it submitted
certifications of permanent defueling pursuant to 10 CFR 50.82(a)(1).
In 2024, Constellation announced its intent to restart Crane, with plans to restore
the operating reactor licensing basis (ORLB) and resume power operations in
2027. While the inspections and testing of ASME Section XI, 10 CFR 50.55a,
and TS 4.4.2 have not been required to be applied at Crane during the
decommissioned period, these requirements will become applicable at Crane
upon returning to the ORLB. Therefore, Crane has elected to complete the RB
ISI scope that would have been required in the 50th Year Surveillance as part of
the plant restart effort. Although completed after the March 9, 2025, the deadline
established by the rolling 5-year window established in ASME Section XI IWL,
this RB ISI is hereafter nominally referred to as the 50th Year Surveillance, or
simply “the surveillance”.
The 50th Year Surveillance was conducted on site from April to June 2026, with
laboratory tests performed in July 2026, finishing July 17, 2026.
This topical report serves as the Engineering Evaluation Report required by
10CFR50.55a, ASME Section XI IWL-3310, and TS 4.4.2.1.6.
The scope for the 50th Year Surveillance was determined in accordance with
requirements in ASME Section XI IWL (ASME XI IWL) and 10CFR50.55a, and is
documented in AR 04831736-02. The tendon sample identified for the

The random sample of tendons drawn for this surveillance includes hoop tendons
initially tensioned from a single-end during construction. As this is the first time
since the second inspection period, special considerations were made as
discussed later in this report.
The Surveillance, performed per Technical Specification 4.4.2.1, conformed to
the requirements of Subsection IWL of Section XI of the ASME Boiler and
Pressure Vessel Code, as incorporated by reference into 10CFR50.55a. The
Surveillance met the requirements as described in the Updated Final Safety
Analysis Report (UFSAR) and was performed in accordance with Crane
Surveillance Procedure 1301-9.1, in addition to Constellation Corporate
Procedures ER-AA-330-005, ER-AA-330-006, ER-AA-335-001, and ER-AA-335-
019. The actual implementation of the surveillance was conducted using
approved vendor procedures.
The Surveillance was comprised of the measurements, examinations, tests and
related activities identified in Section 2, as required by ASME XI IWL.
Surveillance activities also included replacement of two dome tendon end cap
gaskets to eliminate corrosion protection medium (CPM) leaks.
Measurements, examinations and tests on randomly selected tendons had been
performed on a regular basis throughout the life of the plant, on a 5-year rolling
frequency per ASME XI IWL. The exception to this surveillance frequency was
the period at Crane between the completion of the 40th Year Surveillance in 2014
and the start of the 50th Year Surveillance in 2026, during which Crane was
undergoing decommissioning following 2019. Complete examination of the
containment exterior as specified in ASME XI IWL, examination of tendon end
anchorage caps and tendon force trend extrapolation commenced with the
Period 7 surveillance (performed in 2000) in accordance with requirements
introduced in a 1996 amendment to 10CFR50.55a. The Period 11 surveillance is
the sixth to be conducted per 10CFR50.55a and ASME XI IWL. The Period 7,
Period 8, Period 9, 2010 Augmented, and Period 10 Surveillances are
documented in Topical Reports No. 136, 183, 203, 204, and 213 respectively.
The 2010 Augmented Surveillance inspected and tested a small sample of the
tendons affected (de-tensioned / re-tensioned or replaced) by steam generator
replacement activities conducted in 2009.

2. SUMMARY OF WORK PERFORMED AND INSPECTION RESULTS
The work performed during the 50th Year Surveillance and the results of these
examinations and tests are summarized in 2.1 and 2.2 below.

2.1   Work Performed
The 50th Year Surveillance consisted of testing and visual examination of a
randomly selected sample of post-tensioned tendons and a visual examination of
the accessible containment exterior.
The Responsible Engineer (RE) for the surveillance, in accordance with ASME XI
IWL-2320, was Andrew Makinson, P.E.

2.1.1 Sample Selection
ASME XI IWL requires that tendons impacted by repair / replacement activities
be treated as a separate population for sampling and examination purposes.
This population includes those tendons (subsequently identified as SGR
tendons) that were de-tensioned and re-tensioned or replaced in 2009 to
accommodate the access opening for installation of new steam generators.
SGR tendons are sampled and examined as required by IWL-2521.2 and Table
IWL-2521-2. The remaining tendons are sampled and examined in accordance
with Subsection IWL-2520.
The SGR tendons are H46-28 through H46-42 inclusive, H51-28 through H51-42
inclusive, and V113 through V157 inclusive for a total of 30 hoops and 45
verticals. Table IWL-2521-2 specifies that the lesser of 10 tendons or 4% of each
type in the SGR population, hoop and vertical, shall be examined during the first
two inspections following the repair / replacement work. Per Note 6 of Table IWL-
2521-2, if the acceptance in IWL-3221.1 is met for the examined tendons in the
first two surveillances, the required minimum number of tendons examined may
be reduced to the lesser of 5 tendons or 2% of the SGR population for future
surveillances. The 50th Year Surveillance was the 3rd inspection following SGR in
2009, and IWL-3221.1 acceptance criteria was met for examined SGR tendons in
the 2010 Augmented and 40th Year Surveillances, as documented in Topical
Reports 204 and 213, respectively. Consequently, 1 vertical and 1 hoop SGR
tendon were selected for examination during this surveillance.
The non-SGR tendon group sample size is, as specified in Table IWL-2521-1,
the lesser of 5 tendons or 2% of the non-SGR population but at least 3 tendons,
with one tendon in each group being the previously designated control tendon
and the remainder randomly selected. The 50th Year Surveillance also included
additional tendons identified for follow-up examination during previous
surveillance reports.

of SGR tendons, the number of non-SGR tendons and the corresponding

2.1.2 Post-Tensioning System Examinations and Tests
Examinations and tests consisted of the following activities, with exceptions as
noted. These were performed in accordance with Crane Surveillance Procedure
1301-9.1, in addition to Constellation Corporate Procedures ER-AA-330-005, ER-
AA-330-006, ER-AA-335-001, and ER-AA-335-019, which incorporate the
applicable requirements of the 2004 Edition (no Addenda) of the ASME Boiler
and Pressure Vessel Code, Section XI, Subsection IWL and the additional
requirements specified in 10CFR50.55a(b)(2)(viii). The surveillance procedures
also incorporate applicable requirements from the UFSAR. The actual
implementation of surveillance activities is conducted in accordance with the
approved vendor procedures reviewed and approved by the RE and by Crane
Engineering.
   • Collection of corrosion protection medium (CPM) samples from both ends
      of each tendon (samples are not taken if an end cap is removed solely for
      the purpose of gasket repair) and laboratory tests conducted to determine

   • Measurements of end anchorage force (i.e.: “lift-off test”).
   • De-tensioning of one tendon in each non-SGR group (vertical, hoop and

Additionally, all tendon end anchorage covers (End Caps) were examined for

Section XI, Subsection IWL-2510(c).

2.1.3 Containment Surface Examination
The entire accessible exterior surface of the containment was visually examined
in accordance with ASME Section XI, Subsection IWL-2510 using a VT-3C
(general visual) technique. This examination was performed directly (without
optical aids) and remotely using binoculars and an unmanned aircraft system
(UAS). The tendon anchorage end caps and bearing plates were examined at
the same time. The specific conduct of this inspection is governed by ER-AA-
330-005, ER-AA-335-019, and approved vendor procedures.
The concrete was examined for evidence of cracking, spalling, efflorescence,
voids, exposed reinforcing steel, and other types of damage and deterioration as
identified in ACI 201.1R-2008 “Guide for Making a Condition Survey of Concrete
in Service” and ACI 349.3R-2002 “Evaluation of Existing Nuclear Safety-Related
Concrete Structures”. This examination was also focused, as specified in IWL-
2510(c), on CPM seepage through the concrete.
The Bearing plates were examined for detached or missing coatings and
corrosion.
Areas with possible damage or degradation as identified during general visual
examination were re-examined using a VT-1C (detailed visual) technique in
accordance with IWL-2310(b).

2.2      Inspection Results Summary
The results of the 50th Year Reactor Building Surveillance are summarized
below.

2.2.1 Post-Tensioning System
The results of the post-tensioning system examinations, measurements and tests
met all prescriptive acceptance criteria except as noted below. The results are
summarized as follows:
      • The vertical, hoop, and dome tendon measured and normalized group
         mean forces were above the minimum required values, meeting
         acceptance standards in IWL-3221.1(a). As the SGR tendon forces are
         significantly greater than those documented for the other sample tendons,
         these are, for conservatism, not included in the vertical and hoop tendon
         group means.
      • All measured tendon forces were above 95% of predicted value, meeting
         acceptance standards in IWL-3221.1(b).
      • The 95% lower confidence limits on vertical, hoop and dome tendon force
         trends are projected to be above the minimum required mean forces
         beyond 80 years following the RB SIT, thereby meeting acceptance
         standards in IWL-3221.1(c).
      • Elongations measured during the re-tensioning of de-tensioned tendons
         were within 10% of the “as-installed” construction values, meeting
         acceptance standards in IWL-3221.1(d).

3. POST-TENSIONING SYSTEM TESTS AND EXAMINATIONS
The following tests and examinations were performed to assess the continuing
quality and integrity of the post-tensioning system.
      • Measurement of tendon end anchorage forces.
      • Measurement of tendon elongations during re-tensioning.
      • Measurement of wire test specimen strength and elongation at failure.
      • Chemical analysis to determine corrosion protection medium test
         specimen moisture content, reserve alkalinity (base number), and
         concentration of corrosive ions (chlorides, nitrates, and sulfides).
      • Visual examination of the post-tensioning system components, as well as
         the concrete adjacent to the bearing plates, to detect accumulation of free
         water, corrosion, deformation, cracking, wire breakage and wire
         buttonhead failures.
      • Visual examination of the tendon end anchorage covers (end caps) to
         detect damage and corrosion protection medium leakage.
All but the last of the above tests and examinations involved a small sample of
the total tendon population, selected per IWL-2521 as detailed in Section 3.1. In
accordance with ASME XI IWL, 100% of the end caps were visually examined in
their assembled condition.

3.1      Examination Sample Selection
A detailed description of the process for tendon selection in the 50 th Year
Surveillance is documented in AR 04831736-02.
Five sample sets were selected for examination, from two tendon populations.
The larger population included tendons that were not affected by the
repair/replacement activity, which took place during the 2009 steam generator
replacement (SGR) outage, and met the sample size requirements of Table IWL-
2521.1. The smaller population included the tendons affected by the SGR
repair/replacement activity and conformed to the size requirements of Table IWL-
2521-2.
Tendons, except control tendons, initially selected for tests and examinations
were randomly picked from populations (non-SGR and SGR) that included all
tendons not examined during prior surveillances. Control tendons (the SGR
population does not include control tendons) are common to consecutive
surveillances. The non-SGR population consists of three sample sets; vertical,
hoop, and dome tendons. For the 50th Year Surveillance; 3 vertical, 5 hoop and 3
dome tendons were selected. The SGR population consists of two sample sets;
vertical and hoop tendons. For the 50th Year Surveillance; one vertical and one
hoop tendon were selected. Both of the randomly selected SGR tendons were
tendons which were replaced during the SGR outage.

3.2.2 Group Mean Forces
As previously discussed, SGR tendon forces are well above those in the
remaining tendons and are thus conservatively not included in the vertical and
hoop tendon group mean forces.
The mean force in each group of tendons must be equal to or greater than the
minimum required average force for each group as calculated in C-1101-153-
E410-028 and documented in the Crane UFSAR Section 5.7.5.2.3 and Section
9.3.1 of Surveillance Procedure 1301-9.1. The minimum required force values
are:
   • Vertical Tendons:      1,033 kip
   • Hoop Tendons:          1,108 kip
   • Dome Tendons:          1,064 kip
Since these are minimum mean force values, it is expected that the forces of
certain individual tendons will be below these values. This is acceptable in the
Crane design basis provided that the mean forces in the group remain above the
minimum values.
During construction of the containment, individual tendons were tensioned to
anchorage forces between 70% and 73% of GUTS. Differences in initial seating
force are expected to be reflected in the lift-off force measured throughout the life
of the structure.
Also, as tendons were tensioned in sequence, force in any tendon falls (elastic
shortening loss) during the subsequent tensioning of tendons in the same group.
Surveillance samples are quite small, nominally 2% of the tendons in each group.
For this reason, there is a relatively high probability that the samples will consist

projecting tendon forces in ASME XI Code Case N-926. Although N-926 is not

case demonstrates that it has technical basis for use within the industry and can
be relied upon as guidance for projection of Crane’s tendon forces.

3.3   Tendon Elongations and Re-Tensioning
One tendon in each group for both populations (non-SGR and SGR) was de-
tensioned to allow removal of a wire for inspection and testing per IWL-2523.
Tendon elongations were measured during the subsequent re-tensioning, as
required by IWL-2522, and compared to original construction values to verify that
the tendons were intact and that there were no obstructions to tendon motion
within the ducts. Following the elongation measurements at Overstress Force
(OSF), nominally 80% of guaranteed ultimate tensile strength (GUTS), each
tendon was seated, in accordance with IWL-2523.3, between its predicted force
and 70% of GUTS (based on number of effective wires at the time of re-
tensioning).
Tendons V79, V140 (SGR), H51-34 (SGR), H51-52, and D349 were de-
tensioned for wire removal.

3.3.1 Elongations
In accordance with IWL-2522 and approved vendor procedures, elongation for
each re-tensioned tendon was measured from each tendon end at OSF (except
for vertical tendons, where only the top end was measured). These elongation
measurements were adjusted for the number of effective wires in each tendon.
Crane’s RB tendons were originally constructed with 170 total wires, with one
wire being a “surveillance wire”, a small segment of wire placed on each
anchorage that does not carry any pre-stress load. Removing consideration of
the surveillance wire and the wire that was removed from each tendon for
inspection and testing leads to each tendon having 168 effective wires at the time
of re-tensioning. The sums of the elongation measurements from each end were

 1.0 Reason for Evaluation/Scope

        The purpose of this technical evaluation is to evaluate the acceptability of the corrosion protection
        medium (CPM, also referred to as grease) voids on tendons D323, H35-03, H62-26, H13-40, D225,
        and H51-52 which exceeded acceptance standards of ASME Section XI, 2004 Edition, Subsection
        IWL. As part of the 50th Year IWL Reactor Building (RB) Tendon Surveillance at Crane, CPM was
        removed and replaced at tendons D323, H35-03, H62-26, H13-40, D225, and H51-52 in accordance
        with Precision Surveillance Corporation (PSC) Procedure SQ 12.1 and measured as required by IWL-
        2526(a). Only a small amount of grease is removed and replaced from each tendon relative to the
        overall volume of the tendon duct. The absolute difference between the amount of CPM removed
        and the amount replaced in these six tendons was greater than 10% of the tendon net duct volume,
        which exceeds the acceptance standards of IWL-3221.4. Therefore, the grease voids measured in
        these six tendons do not meet acceptance standards of IWL-3221.4 and must be accepted by
        evaluation in accordance with IWL-3310.

        This evaluation was screened per HU-AA-1212. Review of Attachment 2 of HU-AA-1212 identified no
        risk factors, however, as this evaluation pertains to safety related components (the tendons
        themselves), it requires an independent review. An additional review has been performed by the
        Responsible Engineer, Andrew Makinson, P.E., as required by ASME Section XI, 2004 Edition,
        Subsection IWL.

  (c) The acceptability of concrete containment without repair of the item:

      The purpose of filling the tendon duct with grease is to provide corrosion protection for the
      tendon wires and anchorage hardware, especially if there is water intrusion in the tendon duct.
      The horizontal tendon ducts at Crane are made from galvanized steel conduit, and the dome
      tendon ducts are composed of Schedule 40 piping, rather than rolled spiral seam sheet metal
      common at many other containment designs. Additionally, the inner surfaces of the tendon
      ducts conduit are coated with Visconorust 1601 Amber, a heavy wax-based corrosion inhibitor.
      The combination of the galvanized steel conduit (or Schedule 40 Pipe for the dome tendons) and
      corrosion inhibitor make the tendon ducts impervious to water intrusion. As such, the only entry
      point for any water into the tendon duct is at the tendon end caps. During initial tendon
      installation, grease was pumped through the tendon ducts as described above, ensuring that the
      tendon end caps at each end are filled with grease. This is sufficient for preventing water
      intrusion into the tendon ducts that could result in corrosion. The results of previous tendon
      surveillances were reviewed and no free water has been found in end caps, on anchor heads, on
      shims, or on wires. The only exception is tendon V-86 which was discovered with a gap between
      the end cap and bearing plate during the 25th year tendon surveillance. No corrosion was found
      on V-86 hardware items exposed to the water within the end caps or tendon duct. No horizontal
      or dome tendons have had free water discovered during previous surveillances.

      Additionally, each tendon and tendon anchorage was coated with the same heavy wax-based
      corrosion inhibitor (Visconorust 1601 Amber) prior to installation into the tendon conduit,
      providing a layer of corrosion protection separate from the grease. Therefore, a lack of grease
      alone does not mean the tendon hardware was lacking in corrosion protection.

                   inaccessible tendons are not likely to be experiencing hardware corrosion,
                   regardless of their location. The tendons inspected and tested in the 50 th Year and
                   previous surveillances vary in location through the Reactor Building, with dome and
                   vertical tendons surveilled around the RB circumference and horizontal tendons
                   surveilled at numerous elevations including below grade. Therefore, the data from
                   these surveillances is representative. Furthermore, the inaccessible tendons were
                   similarly coated with Visconorust 1601 Amber, which has shown to provide
                   sufficient corrosion resistance even when large grease voids are present. Therefore,
                   the presence of comparable grease voids in inaccessible tendons is acceptable and
                   does not pose a significant degradation risk.

               (3) Description of necessary corrective actions:

                   No corrective actions for Crane’s inaccessible tendons are required as a result of this
                   condition. It is worth noting that each “inaccessible” tendon is accessible for end
                   cap removal from at least one end. If an inaccessible tendon is selected during
                   future tendon surveillances, its anchorage hardware will still be visually examined to
                   the greatest extent practical as required by IWL-2521.1(c). These visual
                   examinations will identify any potential anchorage corrosion, should it be present.

  (d) Whether or not repair/replacement activity is required and, if required, the extent, method, and
      completion date for the repair/replacement activity.

      The tendon ducts for D323, H35-03, H62-26, H13-40, D225, and H51-52 were all refilled with
      sufficient grease during the 50th Year surveillance as required by IWL-2526. Additionally, these
      tendons passed all required ASME Section XI examinations and tests during the current reactor
      building surveillance, demonstrating the grease void had no adverse impact on the ability of the
      tendons to conduct their structural design function. No repair/replacement activities are
      required.

3.0 Conclusion/Findings

   The discussion above supports the conclusion that the observed grease voids for tendon D-323,
   H35-03, H62-26, H13-40, D-225, H51-52 do not have an adverse effect on these tendons, the post
   tensioning system, or concrete containment for Crane Clean Energy Center. The design of the
   tendon ducts at Crane being a galvanized steel conduit, or Schedule 40 piping, internally coated with
   Visconorust 1601 Amber, a heavy wax-based corrosion inhibitor, protects the tendons from water
   intrusion. Additionally, the tendon wires and anchorage hardware are coated with the same heavy
   wax-based corrosion inhibitor which provides additional corrosion protection for post tensioning
   system. Extensive examinations and testing have been performed in accordance with the
   requirements of ASME Section XI, Subsection IWL. The results of the previous examinations and
   tests support the conclusion that the post tensioning system and concrete containment at Crane
   have not experienced any unacceptable degradation impacting the function of the containment.
   Additionally, all examinations and testing during the current 50 th Year IWL Reactor Building Tendon
   surveillance, with the exceptions of the grease voids, satisfy the requirements of ASME Section XI,
   Subsection IWL indicating that this condition has not adversely impacted the function of the
   tendons.
